ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: The head-of-hall reverend is the monastery’s presiding abbot or teacher as named from the community’s institutional side.
EvidenceBody: Pure rules put the title into invitations, announcements, and appointments: a formal notice invites a head-of-hall reverend, a hall attendant announces that he has cancelled evening interview, and a rector cites his instruction when appointing an officer. Reception language asks the head-of-hall reverend at Wuzu to expound before the assembly. Tianyi Yihuai credits such the named teaching figure with close formation and encouragement, while Hongjue Min uses the title when announcing the death of the present monastery’s presiding teacher. The Chan bend is institutional rather than symbolic: the named teaching figure of public encounter is named here as the person who presides over the hall and whose word organizes its communal offices and events.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: The public teacher is designated through the communal hall office: he expounds, cancels interview, authorizes appointments, trains successors, and is mourned as the monastery’s presiding figure.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: The title names the presiding teacher in these records; it is not a synonym for every officer who works in or speaks for the hall.
